Complete Blood Count & Blood Smears

What the analyzer actually measures, which numbers are calculated rather than measured, how to walk the anemia algorithm from a single MCV, and what four real smears look like when the diagnosis is on the slide.

How to use this file

The Most Common Test in Medicine

The complete blood count is one of the most frequently ordered tests there is, which is exactly why it is worth understanding how the numbers are produced. Some are measured, some are calculated, and knowing which is which explains most of the artefacts you will ever see.

Abbreviations used in this file CBC complete blood count · RBC red blood cell, also called an erythrocyte · WBC white blood cell, also called a leukocyte · Hgb hemoglobin · Hct hematocrit — the proportion of blood volume occupied by red cells · MCV mean corpuscular volume — average red cell size · MCH mean corpuscular hemoglobin — average amount of hemoglobin per cell · MCHC mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration — hemoglobin density in the cell · RDW red cell distribution width — how variable the red cell sizes are · MPV mean platelet volume · Retic reticulocyte — an immature red cell still containing RNA · EDTA ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid — the anticoagulant in a lavender-top tube · SLS sodium lauryl sulfate · fL femtolitre (10−15 L) · pg picogram · TIBC total iron binding capacity · TTP thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura · HUS hemolytic uremic syndrome · DIC disseminated intravascular coagulation · TAT turnaround time. LO 1 — Components and workflow

Objective 1

What Is Actually in a Complete Blood Count

Abbreviations in this section CBC complete blood count · RBC / WBC red / white blood cell · MPV mean platelet volume · RDW red cell distribution width · EDTA ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid — the lavender-top anticoagulant · K2 / K3 EDTA the dipotassium / tripotassium salt of EDTA · SD standard deviation · TAT turnaround time · Autoverification automatic release of unflagged, near-normal results without human review.
Cell lineParameters reported
Red blood cellsCount; hemoglobin / hematocrit; MCV / MCH / MCHC (size and content parameters); RDW (distribution width, as standard deviation or percent)
White blood cellsCount; differential (may include immature granulocytes)
PlateletsCount; volume (MPV), immature fraction
Reticulocytes (the immediate red cell precursor)Count, percentage, immature fraction

Slide 4 — Components of the complete blood count, by cell line.

🎙️ What the immature platelet fraction is actually used for

The clinical use given in the recording makes this parameter concrete: monitoring engraftment after a stem cell or bone marrow transplant.

The platelet count itself is still low, but if immature platelets start appearing, the new marrow has begun producing. That is a signal that in two or three days the actual platelet count will start to rise — days of warning you would not otherwise have.

It is the exact platelet analogue of the reticulocyte count: reticulocyte is to red cell as immature platelet fraction is to platelet. Both answer "is the marrow producing?" before the mature count moves.

Two sizing anchors from the same slide, useful at the microscope: red cells and lymphocytes are about the same size on a smear, and a platelet is a cellular fragment, not a full-fledged cell — noticeably smaller than either.

Acceptable specimen criteria

🔑 What the laboratory will and will not accept
  • Fresh whole blood. Ideal within 3 hours of collection; acceptable within 8 hours. Refrigerated samples beyond that point may degrade.
  • EDTA preservative — lavender-top tubes. Two in local use: the Greiner vacutainer (K3 EDTA) and the BD Microtainer (K2 EDTA). In the laboratory's own correlation study, MCV, RDW and hematocrit ran 1–2% higher in the BD tube, but the difference is not likely to be clinically significant.
  • No clots or clumps, which may affect counts. Citrate (blue top) may sometimes be used instead for platelet counts — the workaround for EDTA-dependent platelet clumping, which comes up again in objective 7.
🎙️ Why the phlebotomist inverts the tube — and why a clot ruins the count

EDTA is sprayed on the inside surfaces of the tube, including near the top. If blood simply runs to the bottom and the tube is set down, it never contacts the full dose of anticoagulant — and partial clotting follows. That is why a phlebotomist gently inverts each tube several times after drawing it.

The consequence of getting it wrong: a clot sequesters platelets, and some white and red cells with them. Those cells are no longer in the liquid being analysed, so the counts come back falsely low — and, in the lecture's words, that "could give you an idea that your patient has some kind of disorder, when in fact it's just an artifact from the sample."

One more practical point on the two EDTA tube brands: the 1–2% difference is not clinically significant in isolation, but when you are trending a value over time, use the same tube type — for example following an MCV upward as a patient recovers on iron. Fewer variables, cleaner trend.

🧠 Note the contrast with the coagulation tube

The CBC uses EDTA, which binds calcium irreversibly — fine, because the analyzer only needs to count intact cells. Coagulation testing uses sodium citrate, which binds calcium reversibly so the laboratory can restart clotting on demand. Same principle (remove calcium), opposite requirement, different tube.

The instruments

🔑 The hematology analyzer — Sysmex XN series
  • XN-2000 in the core laboratory; XN-1000 in the satellite laboratory on the hematology/oncology ward.
  • Flow cytometry separates cells based on forward scatter (size) and side scatter (complexity/granularity). This is the single most useful sentence in the methods section: the two scatter axes are what let the machine tell a lymphocyte from a neutrophil.
  • The analyzer counts about 36,000 cells per sample — compare that with the 100–200 cells a technologist counts in a manual differential, which is why the automated count is far more precise.

Slide 6 — The Sysmex analyzer and its scattergram. Forward scatter = size; side scatter = complexity.

Slide 7 — CellaVision. A microscope scanner that rapidly captures cell images and pre-classifies leukocytes.

🧠 Why automation matters — and what it frees people up to do
  • Accuracy — closeness to the "true" result.
  • Precision — reproducibility of measurements over time.
  • Turnaround time — getting correct results quickly to the clinical team, with direct impact on patient and clinic flow.
  • It allows technologists to focus on tasks that improve patient care: smear review for atypical cells such as leukemia blasts, and other special hematology testing that remains manual and time-intensive.
🎙️ Reading the scattergram: which axis is which, and where each cell sits

The orientation used in the lecture: side scatter on the X-axis, forward scatter (with fluorescence) on the Y-axis. Worked through the actual clouds:

  • Lymphocyte — a simple cell: spherical nucleus, thin rim of cytoplasm. So low side scatter and low fluorescence → sits bottom-left.
  • Eosinophil — very bright granules plus a convoluted, lobed nucleus. So very high side scatter → pushed far right.
  • Monocyte — the largest of the normal white cells, so high forward scatter → sits high up.

This is also how the "abnormal scattergram" and "blasts?" flags are generated: blasts and immature cells are larger and cluster somewhere the normal populations do not. When the analyzer finds a dense cloud in unexpected territory, it flags the slide for a human to review.

🪝 Accuracy versus precision — and what each failure implies

The dartboard picture, with a clinical payoff attached:

  • Systematic bias manifests as decreased accuracy — every result is off in the same direction. This may represent an instrument problem, and it is fixable by calibration.
  • Random bias manifests as decreased precision — results scatter around the truth. This may be an intrinsic feature of the assay and may not be fixable at all.

So: consistently wrong → suspect the machine. Inconsistently wrong → suspect the method.

Slide 9 — Accuracy versus precision. Systematic bias hurts accuracy; random bias hurts precision.

🎙️ Putting numbers on precision — and one term worth knowing

Precision is partly a property of the analyte, not just the machine. Two concrete examples given:

  • Platelets fluctuate by roughly 15–20% between repeat runs, intrinsically, because they activate. A repeat count that differs by 15% is not an instrument fault.
  • The MCV is very tightly precise — it varies hardly at all on repeat testing. So a genuinely shifting MCV means something real.

That distinction is exactly the slide's point: some imprecision is intrinsic to the assay and nothing can be done about it, whereas worsening precision in a test that is normally tight suggests an instrument problem.

Turnaround time is also measured across the whole workflow — from the sample arriving to the result reaching the clinician — not just the instrument's run time.

And one term you will meet on a scattergram: ghost cells. These are cells that lysed or died, usually during collection or processing. Having lost their contents and surface markers, they show low forward and low side scatter and cluster at the bottom-left, where the analyzer gates them out as debris. A lot of ghost cells suggests sample degradation — consider a fresh specimen.

Qualitative instrument flags

If there are no flags and results are close to normal ranges, the instrument autoverifies, so results reach providers quickly without human review. Flags are what pull a sample out of that stream and onto a microscope.

Cell typeFlags raised
White blood cellsAbnormal scattergram · Blasts? · Immature granulocytes · Left shift? · Atypical lymphocytes
Red blood cellsAbnormal distribution · Dimorphic population · Anisocytosis · Microcytosis · Macrocytosis · Hypochromia · RBC agglutination · Fragments
PlateletsAbnormal distribution · Platelet clumps?

Q: A hematology analyzer produces platelet counts that are consistently 15% lower than the reference method on every quality control sample. Is this an accuracy or a precision problem, and what does it suggest?

Answer

An accuracy problem, from systematic bias. The results are off by a consistent amount in a consistent direction — which is the definition of systematic bias, and it manifests as decreased accuracy.

The slide states that systematic bias may represent an instrument problem, so the next step is calibration and instrument troubleshooting. If instead the results scattered widely around the correct value, that would be random bias reducing precision, which may be an intrinsic feature of the assay rather than a fault.

LO 2 — Methodology

Objective 2

How Each Value Is Actually Obtained

Abbreviations in this section SLS sodium lauryl sulfate — the cyanide-free hemoglobin reagent · SLS-HGB the coloured SLS–hemoglobin complex read at 555 nm · nm nanometre — the unit of wavelength · AC alternating current · MCV mean corpuscular volume · MPV mean platelet volume · PLT-F the fluorescent platelet channel · CD41 / CD61 platelet glycoprotein IIb / IIIa — the flow cytometry reference markers · RNA ribonucleic acid — what reticulocyte stains detect · µL microlitre.

Four measurement principles cover the whole panel: a colour reaction for hemoglobin, impedance for counting and sizing, flow cytometry for the differential, and fluorescence for the difficult platelet counts.

Hemoglobin — a photometric colour reaction

🔑 Cyanide-free sodium lauryl sulfate (SLS) method
  1. SLS lyses red blood cells and white blood cellsHemoglobin is released into solution.
  2. The heme group undergoes oxidation
  3. SLS hydrophilic groups bind heme, forming a stable coloured complex (SLS-HGB)
  4. SLS-HGB is measured photometrically at 555 nmThat specific wavelength is chosen to minimise interference from turbidity and other compounds — which is the hook for objective 7, where lipemia and high white counts make the sample cloudy.

Note the "cyanide-free" in the name: the older reference method converted hemoglobin to cyanmethemoglobin, which meant handling and disposing of cyanide reagent. SLS avoids that.

Slide 12 — Hemoglobin by SLS. Lyse, oxidise, complex, then read absorbance at 555 nm.

🎙️ What the analyzer is measuring, structurally

Worth pinning down what is being detected: hemoglobin is four globin chains, each cradling a heme group, and each heme holds the iron atom that binds oxygen. Lysing the cell releases that whole molecule into solution, and the SLS complex is what gives it a measurable absorbance.

Why it matters clinically: this is the number that defines anemia, and the downstream logic is less hemoglobin → less oxygen delivered → hypoxia → anaerobic metabolism, and if severe and sustained, tissue death.

Hematocrit — the traditional measurement

🧠 Spun hematocrit

A centrifuge separates the denser red cells from plasma, and the proportion of the tube occupied by red cells is the hematocrit. This is the original physical measurement, and it is still the reference standard.

The modern analyzer does not do this. It calculates the hematocrit as Hct = (RBC × MCV) / 10. That distinction matters: anything that corrupts the red cell count or the MCV propagates directly into the hematocrit — which is precisely what happens with cold agglutinins in objective 7.

Slide 13 — The spun hematocrit. The physical measurement the calculated value replaced.

🎙️ The rule of three — hematocrit ≈ 3 × hemoglobin

A quick bedside check not on the slides: the hematocrit runs at roughly three times the hemoglobin. Hemoglobin 10 g/dL → expect a hematocrit near 30%.

The important qualifier: this holds only when the MCV is normal. The two are linked through cell size, so when cells are unusually small or large the ratio drifts — and a hemoglobin and hematocrit that do not fit the rule of three is itself a finding, pointing either at abnormal red cell size or at one of the interferences in objective 7.

Cell counting by impedance — the Coulter principle

🔑 The Coulter principle in one sentence

Cells suspended in a conductive fluid are drawn through a narrow aperture. When a cell crosses it, the cell is sensed through a change in impedance (resistance in an alternating current circuit), and the size of the impedance change is proportional to the cell's size.

So one measurement gives two things at once: each pulse is one cell (the count) and the pulse height is that cell's volume (the size).

  • For red cells: provides the count and MCV.
  • For platelets: provides the count and MPV.
  • For white cells: provides the count — the differential comes from flow cytometry, not impedance.

Slide 14 — The Coulter principle. Each cell crossing the aperture makes a pulse; pulse height is cell size.

🪝 Why impedance sizing is the root of most CBC artefacts

The machine decides what a cell is almost entirely from how big it is. So anything that is the wrong size for its identity gets misclassified, and this single idea explains the whole platelet-counting problem below and most of objective 7:

  • Other cells mistaken for platelets — schistocytes, microcytes, white cell fragments. All small, so all counted as platelets, falsely raising the platelet count.
  • Platelets mistaken for other cells — platelet clumps and large or giant platelets. Too big to be platelets, so they are missed, falsely lowering the platelet count.
🎙️ Inside the aperture — and why there is more than one

The physical set-up: a conductive bath with a charge across a small pore. Cells are drawn through the pore one at a time, and each passage changes the resistance between the two chambers, producing a blip in the monitored voltage. Count the blips → the cell count. Measure each blip's height → that cell's size.

The analyzer then plots the distribution of those heights, and that curve is where the MCV and the RDW come from: the MCV is the mean of the distribution, and the RDW is how wide it is.

Critically, there is more than one aperture, sized for the population being counted — a small pore for platelets, a mid-size one for red cells, a larger one for white cells. That is the design assumption the interferences in objective 7 exploit: anything the wrong size for its identity goes through the wrong pore and is counted as the wrong thing.

Fluorescent platelet counting — the fix

🔑 PLT-F: staining rather than sizing
  • Analyzes about 80 µL of sample.
  • Stains platelet rough endoplasmic reticulum and mitochondria with a specific fluorescent dye (oxazine) and measures fluorescent intensity — identifying platelets by what they contain rather than by how big they are.
  • Uses an extended count volume and extended count time, so more platelets are counted and the statistical precision improves.
  • Correlates well with CD41/CD61 expression — the flow cytometry reference method (and note those are the same glycoproteins, GPIIb/IIIa, that are absent in Glanzmann thrombasthenia).
  • Distinguishes immature from mature platelets — the immature platelet fraction, which is to platelets what the reticulocyte count is to red cells.
  • Especially useful for low counts (<50 ×103/µL), which is exactly where the transfusion decision sits.

Reticulocyte count

🔑 Reticulocytes — staining the leftover RNA
  • A stain that highlights RNA differentiates reticulocytes from mature red cells. A reticulocyte is an immature red cell that has expelled its nucleus but still contains RNA; a mature red cell has neither.
  • Normal range roughly 0.8–4%.
  • Used to evaluate the compensatory response to anemia. The question it answers: is the anemia due to low production or to increased cellular destruction?

Slide 15 — Reticulocyte count. RNA staining separates immature from mature red cells.

🎙️ Nucleated red cells — why a red cell has a nucleus at all, and why losing it matters

A red cell is born with a nucleus, because it needs one to manufacture its hemoglobin. Once it is fully loaded, the nucleus has no further use and gets in the way, so the cell ejects it. A reticulocyte is the stage just after that, still carrying leftover RNA; a mature red cell has neither.

So a nucleated red cell in the peripheral blood is a cell released before it was finished. That means either the marrow is under stress and rushing output, or something is taking over the marrow and forcing cells out — metastasis, fibrosis. Either way it warrants explanation.

Two consequences worth carrying: the reticulocyte stain is the same basic dye that stains white cell nuclei (both target nucleic acid), and because nucleated red cells have nuclei, the analyzer will count them as white cells unless it corrects for them — one of the interferences in objective 7.

The same fact explains a disease from the hemolytic anemia lecture: because the red cell has no nucleus, the G6PD it carries at birth is all it will ever have. It cannot make more, so a deficient cell runs out of oxidant protection partway through its life.

🪝 The reticulocyte count is the single most useful add-on to an anemia workup

High reticulocytes = the marrow is working, so the cells are being lost — hemolysis or bleeding. Low reticulocytes = the marrow is the problem — iron, B12 or folate deficiency, renal failure, marrow failure. It is the branch point in the normocytic column of the anemia algorithm in objective 3, and it costs almost nothing to add.

Slide 17 — Summary of methodologies. Impedance, flow cytometry, photometry and fluorescence, side by side.

Q: A patient with severe iron deficiency and marked microcytosis has an automated platelet count of 610,000/µL, but the smear shows only a moderate number of platelets. Explain the discrepancy and how the laboratory would resolve it.

Answer

Microcytes are being counted as platelets. Impedance counting assigns identity by size, and the slide lists microcytes alongside schistocytes and white cell fragments among the "other cells that may be mistaken for platelets". In severe iron deficiency the red cells become small enough to fall into the platelet size window, falsely elevating the count.

Resolution is to count by a method that does not depend on size: the fluorescent (PLT-F) channel, which stains platelet rough endoplasmic reticulum and mitochondria with oxazine and identifies platelets by their contents. It correlates well with CD41/CD61 flow cytometry and is specifically useful at the extremes of the count.

Q: Which CBC parameters are directly measured and which are calculated?

Answer

Measured: the red cell count and MCV (both from impedance — one pulse per cell, pulse height for size), and the hemoglobin (photometrically at 555 nm as the SLS-hemoglobin complex).

Calculated:

  • Hct = (RBC × MCV) / 10
  • MCH = (Hgb / RBC) × 10
  • MCHC = (Hgb / Hct) × 100
  • RDW = standard deviation of volume / MCV

This matters because an error in a measured value propagates into every value derived from it. Cold agglutinins that clump red cells drop the count and inflate the MCV, and the calculated hematocrit and MCHC both go wrong as a direct consequence — which is why an impossibly high MCHC is such a reliable red flag.

LO 3 — Diagnostic information

Objective 3 · part 1

Red Cell Indices and the Anemia Algorithm

Abbreviations in this section MCV mean corpuscular volume — average red cell size · MCH mean corpuscular hemoglobin — average amount of hemoglobin per cell · MCHC mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration — hemoglobin density · RDW red cell distribution width — variation in cell size · fL femtolitre (10−15 L) · pg picogram · Retics reticulocytes · Hgb E hemoglobin E, a structural hemoglobin variant · Hb-opathies hemoglobinopathies · Enzymopathies / membranopathies red cell enzyme and membrane defects.
🔑 The indices, with normal adult ranges and formulas
IndexMeasured or calculatedFormulaNormal adult rangeWhat it means
RBC — red cell countMeasured—3.5–5.5 ×106/µLHow many cells
Hgb — hemoglobinMeasured—14–18 g/dL (male); 12–16 g/dL (female)Oxygen-carrying capacity — the number that defines anemia
MCV — mean corpuscular volumeMeasured—80–100 fLAverage red cell size. Values are lower in children

🧠 MCH versus MCHC — the pair students reliably confuse

MCH is an amount; MCHC is a concentration. A cell can contain little hemoglobin because it is small (low MCH, normal MCHC) or because it is underfilled for its size (low MCHC — true hypochromia). Because MCHC is a density, it is bounded by physics, and that is what makes it such a useful artefact detector: a reported MCHC above about 37 g/dL is usually impossible and points at a laboratory interference, not a disease.

🎙️ Reference ranges shift with age — a paediatric laboratory carries several

Because this is a children's hospital laboratory, the computer system holds multiple reference ranges and applies the right one by age — a 3-year-old and an 18-year-old are not compared against the same numbers.

The example given is the one already flagged in the table: the MCV is lower in children than in adults. Reading a paediatric MCV against an adult range will manufacture a microcytosis that is not there.

Size abnormalities and what they mean

FindingDefinitionCauses
MicrocytesCells smaller than normal (MCV <80 fL)Iron deficiency, thalassemia, lead poisoning, sideroblastic anemias. Often associated with hypochromia — fainter staining showing reduced hemoglobin content
MacrocytesCells larger than normal (MCV >100 fL)Vitamin B12 deficiency, folate deficiency, liver disease
AnisocytosisA combination of both — variation in sizeReflected in a raised RDW
⚠️ The averaging trap — why the MCV can lie

The MCV is an average, and averages hide bimodal data. The lecture makes the point explicitly: the MCV may be normal, but the smear might show dual populations. Two named scenarios:

  • Microcytic anemia with a brisk reticulocytosis — small cells averaged with large young ones.
  • After transfusion of normal blood into a microcytic patient — the patient's small cells averaged with the donor's normal ones.

The tell is a raised RDW with a normal MCV, and the confirmation is looking at the smear. This is the strongest argument in the lecture for why the smear still exists.

The anemia algorithm

🔑 Diagnosis of anemia — the practical approach

Start with a low hemoglobin, then split on the MCV. In the normocytic column only, split again on the reticulocyte count.

🪝 Two details on this algorithm that are exam gold
  • Thalassemia may show an increased red cell count. This is the cleanest way to separate it from iron deficiency at the CBC alone. Both are microcytic and both have a low hemoglobin, but in thalassemia the marrow makes many small cells (RBC count normal or high), whereas in iron deficiency it makes few small cells (RBC count low). Iron studies confirm it — and critically, giving iron to a thalassemia trait patient achieves nothing and risks overload.
  • Chronic disease and sideroblastic anemia appear in two columns. They are bracketed in the microcytic column and listed plainly in the normocytic one because they usually start normocytic and only become microcytic later. If they do not fit the first column you try, try the other.

Q: Two patients both have a hemoglobin of 10.5 g/dL and an MCV of 68 fL. Patient A has a red cell count of 3.1 ×106/µL; patient B has 6.2 ×106/µL. What is the likely diagnosis in each, and why does the distinction matter urgently?

Answer

Patient A: iron deficiency anemia. Few cells, and they are small — the marrow cannot build hemoglobin, so it builds fewer, smaller cells.

Patient B: thalassemia. The algorithm notes that thalassemia may see an increased RBC count — the marrow produces plenty of cells, each of which is small and underfilled.

It matters because the treatments are opposite. Patient A needs iron. Patient B has normal or high iron stores, gains nothing from supplementation, and is put at risk of iron overload by it. Confirm with iron studies (ferritin, total iron binding capacity) and hemoglobin electrophoresis.

Q: A patient has a normocytic anemia. What single inexpensive test most efficiently divides the differential, and what does each result mean?

Answer

The reticulocyte count — it is the branch point in the normocytic column of the algorithm. Normal range roughly 0.8–4%.

  • High reticulocytes → the marrow is responding, so the cells are being destroyed or lost: hemolysis, recovery from an insult, hemoglobinopathies, enzymopathies, membranopathies.
  • Low reticulocytes → the marrow itself is the problem: renal failure (no erythropoietin), chronic disease, sideroblastic anemia, hypoendocrine states, aplastic anemia, or a mixed deficiency.

The question it answers, in the lecture's own words: is the anemia due to low production or increased cellular destruction?

LO 3 — The smear

Objective 3 · part 2

Preparing and Reading a Peripheral Smear

Abbreviations in this section Monolayer the region of a smear where cells sit evenly spaced without overlapping — the only place morphology should be read · Feather edge the thin trailing end of a smear · Wright–Giemsa the standard peripheral smear stain (eosin + methylene blue) · DNA deoxyribonucleic acid.
🔑 The three regions of a smear — and where to actually look
  • The feather edge — the thin trailing end. Cells are spread too far apart and distorted; large cells preferentially collect here.
  • The thicker edge — cells overlap and are piled up; morphology is uninterpretable.
  • The monolayer, between the two — the best morphology is where cells are evenly distributed without touching or overlapping. This is the only region you should assess morphology in.

The HemaPrep automated spreader ensures a consistent smear, which is needed for CellaVision — the image-capture system cannot compensate for a badly made slide.

Slide 23 — Smear preparation and the regions of a smear. Read the monolayer, not the feather edge.

🎙️ What a normal red cell actually is, and where the central pallor comes from

The mental model offered: a donut whose hole is filled in. The centre is thinner, not absent — and that dip is where the nucleus used to be before the cell ejected it. Because cells settle flat on the slide and you view them top-down, that thin centre reads as the central pallor.

Normal central pallor occupies about one third of the cell. Notably wider than that is hypochromia — the concrete threshold behind the "faint staining" description.

And the reason the shape exists at all: the biconcave disc bends and twists. Capillaries are sometimes narrower than the red cell's own diameter, so the cell has to deform to get through. That is precisely what fails in sickle cell disease, where the cells are stiff and deformed — and it is why spherocytes, having lost that flexibility, are pulled out by the spleen.

Stains — why blood cells have colour at all

🧠 Wright–Giemsa, and the acid–base logic behind it

Individual cells are translucent — without a stain there is essentially nothing to see. Two dyes with opposite charges pick out opposite compartments:

  • Hematoxylin — a basic dye that stains acidic material, for example DNA in the nucleus. Blue/purple.
  • Eosin — an acidic dye that stains basic material, for example protein in the cytoplasm. Pink/orange.

The Wright–Giemsa stain used for peripheral smears combines eosin and methylene blue. Devised in 1902, and named for James Homer Wright (American pathologist) and Gustav Giemsa (German chemist and bacteriologist).

🎙️ A clarification worth making explicit

The red you see on a smear is the eosin, not the hemoglobin. An individual red cell is essentially translucent — it is only when you pile enough of them together, as in a tube of blood, that you see red. On a monolayer smear the colour is entirely the dye you added.

Convenient that eosin happens to stain red cells a red-orange, but it is a coincidence of chemistry: eosin binds protein, and a red cell is essentially a bag of protein.

🪝 Memory hook — opposites attract

A basic dye binds acidic targets, and an acidic dye binds basic targets. So the nucleus (acidic DNA) goes blue and the cytoplasm (basic protein) goes pink. That is also where the granulocyte names come from: an eosinophil loves the acidic dye eosin and its granules are bright orange-red; a basophil loves the basic dye and goes dark blue-purple; a neutrophil is indifferent to both and stains a neutral pale lilac.

  1. Microscopic featuresWhat is actually on the slide.
  2. PathophysiologyWhy the cells look like that.
  3. Clinical implicationsWhat it means for the patient.
  4. Other laboratory studiesWhat to send next to confirm.

Q: A trainee assesses red cell morphology at the feather edge of a smear and reports numerous spherocytes. Why is that report unreliable?

Answer

Because morphology must be read in the monolayer — the region where cells are evenly distributed without touching or overlapping. The feather edge is the thin trailing end, where cells are dragged out and distorted by the spreading process and where large cells preferentially collect.

Red cells at the feather edge characteristically lose their central pallor as an artefact of being flattened and over-spread — which is precisely the feature that defines a spherocyte. Reading there manufactures spherocytes that are not present.

The other extreme, the thicker edge, is equally useless because cells pile up and overlap. This is also why the HemaPrep automated spreader matters: it ensures a consistent smear, which CellaVision requires in order to capture and pre-classify cells reliably.

Q: Why does a nucleus stain blue and cytoplasm stain pink, and how does that naming logic extend to eosinophils and basophils?

Answer

Because opposites attract. Hematoxylin is a basic dye that stains acidic material — nuclear DNA is acidic, so the nucleus goes blue-purple. Eosin is an acidic dye that stains basic material — cytoplasmic protein is basic, so the cytoplasm goes pink-orange. Without a stain, individual cells are translucent and essentially invisible.

The granulocytes are named for which dye their granules prefer: an eosinophil takes up the acidic dye eosin and its granules are bright orange-red; a basophil takes up the basic dye and goes dark blue-purple; a neutrophil is indifferent to both and stains a neutral pale lilac.

The peripheral smear stain is Wright–Giemsa, combining eosin and methylene blue, devised in 1902 and named for James Homer Wright and Gustav Giemsa.

Objective 3 · part 3

Four Smear Cases Where the Diagnosis Is on the Slide

Abbreviations in this section TIBC total iron binding capacity — rises in iron deficiency · Ferritin the iron storage protein; the best marker of iron stores · HbSS homozygous sickle cell disease · Glu → Val glutamate replaced by valine — the sickle mutation · Polychromasia blue-grey young red cells on the smear; the smear equivalent of a raised reticulocyte count · TTP thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura · HUS hemolytic uremic syndrome · DIC disseminated intravascular coagulation · MAHA microangiopathic hemolytic anemia · Parasitaemia the percentage of red cells infected · cc/kg millilitres per kilogram of body weight.

Case 1 — an 18-month-old with fatigue

🔑 Microscopic features and presentation

Decreased red cell number and hemoglobin. Microcytic, hypochromic cells.
18-month-old child with fatigue. Hemoglobin 4.6 g/dL, MCV 58 fL.

Slide 27 — Case 1. Microcytic, hypochromic red cells with wide central pallor.

🩺 The full case — severe iron deficiency anemia
TestPatient valueNormal rangeDirection
Hemoglobin3.6 g/dL10.2–12.7 g/dLVery low
TIBC (total iron binding capacity)421 mcg/dL160–415 mcg/dLHigh — more transferrin, hunting for iron
Ferritin1 ng/mL10–500 ng/mLEssentially absent — stores are empty
Hemoglobin electrophoresisNormal—Excludes a hemoglobinopathy

Management: transfused a total of 15 cc/kg red cells, expected to raise the hemoglobin by about 3 g/dL. Started on oral ferrous sulfate and restricted milk products.

🪝 Why milk restriction is the treatment, not an aside

Excessive cow's milk intake in a toddler is a classic cause of iron deficiency by three separate mechanisms: it is low in iron, its calcium and casein inhibit absorption of what iron there is, and it can cause occult gastrointestinal blood loss. Giving iron without addressing the milk treats the number rather than the cause.

Note also the transfusion arithmetic worth carrying: roughly 10–15 cc/kg of red cells raises hemoglobin by about 2–3 g/dL. In chronic severe anemia the child has compensated, so transfusion is deliberately slow and partial.

🎙️ The transfusion target, and why milk is the disease

The stated goal was to get the hemoglobin closer to 7 — not to normal. In chronic, slowly developing anemia the child has physiologically compensated, so transfusion is deliberately partial and cautious; the marrow does the rest once given iron.

And the mechanism behind the milk restriction: at this age a diet dominated by milk and other iron-poor foods, in a child who is growing fast, means iron demand outruns intake. Reserves are used up over months — "a chronic process that develops over several months" — which is exactly why the hemoglobin can fall to 3.6 g/dL before anyone notices.

Case 2 — a 5-year-old with a history of pain crises

🔑 Microscopic features and presentation

Decreased red cell number. Target cells and sickle cells. Polychromasia.
5-year-old with anemia and a history of pain crises and splenic sequestration.

Polychromasia — blue-grey cells on the smear — is the morphological equivalent of a raised reticulocyte count: young cells still carrying RNA. It tells you the marrow is responding, which fits a hemolytic process.

Slide 29 — Case 2. Sickle cells, target cells and polychromasia.

🩺 The full case

5-year-old male with hemoglobin SS disease and a history of acute chest syndrome, maintained on hydroxyurea. Admitted with fever 39.3 °C, white cell count 36,000/µL, and streptococcal pharyngitis.

Treatment: ceftriaxone, paracetamol/acetaminophen, hydration, albuterol and budesonide.

Confirmed with a sickle cell solubility test.

Slide 30 — The sickle solubility test. Deoxygenated hemoglobin S precipitates and turns the solution turbid.

🧠 The pathophysiology
  • Mutation in the hemoglobin β-chain: β6 Glu → Val — glutamate replaced by valine, which is more hydrophobic. That hydrophobic patch lets deoxygenated hemoglobin S molecules polymerise into rigid fibres that deform the cell.
  • Gene frequency around 4% in African-Americans.
  • Sickling is worsened by hypoxia and dehydration — both increase the proportion of deoxygenated hemoglobin and its intracellular concentration.
  • A severe, debilitating illness affecting multiple organs with decreased life expectancy.

Slide 31 — Sickle cell disease. β6 Glu→Val, hydrophobic polymerisation, multi-organ disease.

⚠️ Why fever in sickle cell disease is an emergency

These patients are functionally asplenic from repeated infarction, so they cannot clear encapsulated organisms — Streptococcus pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, Neisseria meningitidis. That is why the treatment here starts with ceftriaxone rather than observation: fever is treated as presumed sepsis until proven otherwise. It is also why hydration is on the list — dehydration directly worsens sickling.

🎙️ Target cells on a smear? Send a hemoglobin electrophoresis

Asked live whether thalassemia can be identified from the smear, the answer was a clear no: you cannot differentiate these conditions from morphology alone.

The rule that follows was repeated twice and is the single most actionable next-step in this lecture: if you see a lot of target cells, send a hemoglobin electrophoresis. It identifies the hemoglobin variant and establishes whether a thalassemia is present.

Target cells are a feature of hemoglobin disorders generally — thalassemias and hemoglobinopathies alike — and combinations exist, such as hemoglobin S with beta thalassemia, or hemoglobin S with hemoglobin C. Only electrophoresis separates them.

Case 3 — a 17-year-old with bruising and confusion

🔑 Microscopic features and presentation

Decreased red cell number. Increased schistocytes.
17-year-old female with bruising, fever, acute mental status change, and a low platelet count.

Slide 32 — Case 3. Schistocytes at 100×.

🩺 Schistocytes in thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura

Schistocytes are fragments of red cells without central pallor and with two pointed ends. They are the morphological signature of a microangiopathic hemolytic anemia — cells physically sheared as they are forced past intravascular strands.

The causes listed in this lecture:

  • TTP, hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS), atypical HUS
  • Obstetric complications — amniotic fluid embolism
  • Malignant hypertension
  • March hemoglobinuria — mechanical destruction from repetitive impact
  • Disseminated intravascular coagulation (DIC)
  • Shearing due to heart valves

Slide 33 — Schistocytes in TTP. Fragments without central pallor, with two pointed ends.

🪝 This case is the bridge to the coagulation lectures

The presentation here — bruising, fever, mental status change, thrombocytopenia, schistocytes — is TTP, covered mechanistically in Coagulation Part II as ADAMTS13 failure. The discriminator to carry across: in TTP the PT and aPTT are normal; in DIC both are prolonged and fibrinogen falls. The smear looks the same in both; the coagulation panel does not.

🎙️ The TTP pentad

TTP classically presents with a pentad, and this case supplies four of the five:

  1. Fever
  2. ThrombocytopeniaHence the bruising.
  3. Microangiopathic hemolytic anemiaThe schistocytes.
  4. Neurological changesThe acute mental status change.
  5. Renal impairment

But the practical instruction is not to wait for all five. Recognition has improved to the point that anyone with some of these features, or with schistocytes, should be treated as TTP while confirmatory results are pending — because untreated TTP kills, and plasma exchange works.

Case 4 — a 5-year-old back from Afghanistan

🔑 Microscopic features and presentation

5-year-old who recently travelled to Afghanistan and was bitten by mosquitoes. Periodic fevers, fatigue, nausea.

ValueResultNote
Hemoglobin10.7 g/dLMild anemia
Hematocrit31.9%
MCV70 fLMicrocytic
White cell count11.47 ×103/µLReactive lymphocytes present; granulocytes left-shifted
Platelets47 ×103/µLLow — the finding that should trigger the thought

Slide 34 — Case 4. Intraerythrocytic parasites on the smear.

🩺 Plasmodium — malaria
  • Parasite load: 1.8% of red cells infected. Quantifying parasitaemia is part of the report, not optional — it drives treatment intensity.
  • Morphology is suggestive of Plasmodium vivax infection.
  • BinaxNOW rapid antigen test shows a band for the P. vivax, P. malariae, P. ovale common antigen and is negative for P. falciparum.

Slide 35 — Plasmodium vivax. Parasite load 1.8%.

🎙️ Malaria specifics from the recording
  • Five species of Plasmodium infect humans.
  • In this P. vivax case the forms seen were mature schizonts — the parasite progressively taking over the cell and consuming its hemoglobin. P. vivax is milder and is more common in Afghanistan.
  • P. falciparum is "the one to remember" — most aggressive, most widespread. Its smear shows many more ring forms, with occasional gametocytes. Severe cases run parasitaemia of 15–20%.
⚠️ Plasmodium falciparum — the one that kills

A separate case: a child who had recently returned from Cameroon.

  • The most virulent species.
  • Can present with parasitaemia levels above 10% — compare the 1.8% in the vivax case. P. falciparum infects red cells of all ages, whereas P. vivax prefers young cells, which caps its parasitaemia.

This is exactly why species identification and a parasite count are both required, and why the negative falciparum band on the rapid test in case 4 was reassuring.

Slide 36 — Plasmodium falciparum. The most virulent species; parasitaemia can exceed 10%.

🎙️ Why sickle cell, G6PD deficiency and thalassemia are all still common

Raised as a student question and answered as "a great question": these disorders persist at high frequency because being heterozygous confers protection against malaria — the red cells are, in the lecturer's phrase, "less hospitable" to the parasite. A real evolutionary advantage in malarial regions, paid for by the severe disease in homozygotes.

There is a neat closing of the loop with the white cell lecture: the Duffy antigen is the receptor P. vivax uses to enter red cells, so Duffy-null individuals are resistant to P. vivax — and the Duffy-null phenotype is the same one that gives a constitutionally lower neutrophil count. The same malaria pressure shaped both the red cell and the white cell findings.

🪝 The pattern that should make you request a malaria smear

Fever + travel + thrombocytopenia. Thrombocytopenia is present in the large majority of malaria cases and is one of the most consistent laboratory clues — in case 4 the platelet count of 47,000 is the abnormality that stands out. Add the periodic fever pattern and the mosquito exposure, and the smear is mandatory.

Q: A patient's smear shows schistocytes and the platelet count is low. What two laboratory results would you look at immediately to separate a thrombotic microangiopathy from disseminated intravascular coagulation?

Answer

The PT/aPTT and the fibrinogen.

  • TTP, HUS and aHUS: PT and aPTT normal, fibrinogen normal. The clotting factors are not being consumed — the problem is platelets and endothelium.
  • DIC: PT and aPTT both prolonged, fibrinogen low or falling, with a markedly raised D-dimer.

The smear cannot make this distinction — schistocytes appear in every entry on the list (TTP, HUS, aHUS, obstetric complications, malignant hypertension, march hemoglobinuria, DIC, mechanical valves). The coagulation panel can, in one look.

Q: Why does the report in case 4 state the parasite load as a percentage, and why does species identification change management?

Answer

Parasitaemia quantifies severity and is followed to judge response to therapy. Case 4 was 1.8%; the comparison case notes that P. falciparum can present with parasitaemia above 10%.

Species matters because P. falciparum is the most virulent species — it is the one that causes cerebral malaria and death, it can reach far higher parasite loads, and it is treated more aggressively. The BinaxNOW rapid test distinguishes it: in case 4 the band was for the vivax/malariae/ovale common antigen and the falciparum band was negative.

P. vivax and P. ovale additionally form dormant liver hypnozoites, so they require treatment aimed at preventing relapse as well as clearing the blood stage.

Eight shapes worth recognising on sight. The lecture presents them as two panels of four; the table below adds what each one means, since the shape is only useful if it points somewhere.

Slide 37 — Spherocytes, ovalo(ellipto)cytes, stomatocytes, tear drop cells (dacryocytes).

MorphologyWhat it looks likeClassically associated with
SpherocytesSmall, round, densely stained, no central pallorHereditary spherocytosis; autoimmune hemolytic anemia — membrane removed by splenic macrophages
Ovalocytes / elliptocytesOval to cigar-shapedHereditary elliptocytosis; also iron deficiency and myelodysplasia
StomatocytesCentral pallor is a slit or "mouth" rather than roundHereditary stomatocytosis; alcohol and liver disease
Tear drop cells (dacryocytes)One pointed end, like a teardropMyelofibrosis; marrow infiltration; also thalassemia. Squeezed as they exit a scarred marrow
Target cells (codocytes)A bullseye — central dot of hemoglobin inside the pallorThalassemia, hemoglobin C, liver disease, post-splenectomy — excess membrane relative to contents
Hemoglobin C crystalsDense, angular, rod- or bar-shaped intracellular crystalsHemoglobin C disease
Acanthocytes (spur cells)Few, irregular, unevenly spaced blunt projectionsSevere liver disease, abetalipoproteinemia, post-splenectomy
Echinocytes (burr cells)Many, regular, evenly spaced short spiculesUremia / renal failure; also a common artefact of slow drying or storage

PolychromasiaLarger, blue-grey cellsReticulocytes — the smear equivalent of a raised reticulocyte count; means the marrow is responding
🎙️ The shortest version of the spiky-cell rule

Given in the recording as a single line: burr cells point to kidney disorders, spur cells point to liver disorders.

Two more notes from the same run-through: spherocytes arise either from antibody-mediated hemolysis or from inherited spherocytosis, where the cells are constitutionally more fragile; and hemoglobin C, which also occurs in African populations, causes mild hemolysis with target cells and a very pale appearance — and can be inherited alongside hemoglobin S as HbSC disease.

🪝 The pair worth being able to separate: acanthocyte versus echinocyte

Both are spiky. Acanthocyte = few, irregular, uneven spicules → think liver. Echinocyte = many, regular, even spicules → think kidney (uremia), or an artefact. Mnemonic: acanthocyte has asymmetric spikes; echinocyte has even ones. The echinocyte's status as a common drying artefact is the practical reason it is worth telling them apart — one is a finding, the other is often just a badly handled slide.

🧠 Target cells — one mechanism, several diseases

A target cell has too much membrane for the amount of haemoglobin inside, so the excess surface folds into a central bump. That happens either because the contents are reduced (thalassemia, iron deficiency) or because the membrane is increased (liver disease, where lipid loading expands the membrane; post-splenectomy, where the spleen is no longer trimming cells). Same final shape, opposite starting points.

Q: A smear shows numerous cells with many short, evenly spaced projections. The clinician insists the patient has liver disease. What do you tell them?

Answer

Many, regular, evenly spaced spicules describe an echinocyte (burr cell), not an acanthocyte. Echinocytes point toward uremia / renal failure — or, very commonly, toward a preparation artefact from slow drying, prolonged storage before smearing, or a pH problem with the stain.

The liver disease cell is the acanthocyte (spur cell), which has few, irregular, unevenly spaced blunt projections.

Practically: check renal function, and check when and how the slide was made. If the sample sat before smearing, request a fresh specimen — the lecture's closing point is that in some cases you may need to redraw the specimen.

LO 4 — Interferences

Objective 4

Interferences and Troubleshooting

Abbreviations in this section MCHC mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration — the best single artefact detector · Pseudothrombocytopenia a falsely low platelet count from EDTA-dependent clumping · PLT-F the fluorescent platelet channel · nRBC nucleated red blood cell · Lipemia turbid, fat-laden plasma · Cold agglutinin an antibody that clumps red cells at low temperature · Hyperbilirubinemia raised plasma bilirubin, which adds pigment and absorbance.

The fourth objective, and the one that makes the rest of the lecture practical. Every interference below follows from something already covered: the analyzer identifies cells by size, reads hemoglobin by absorbance, and calculates several of the numbers it reports.

InterferenceWhat it does to the CBCMechanismHow to resolve it
Platelet clumping (EDTA-dependent)Falsely low platelet count; may falsely raise the white countClumps are too large to be sized as platelets, so they are missed — or counted as leukocytes. Flagged as "Platelet clumps?"Redraw in citrate (blue top) — named in the specimen criteria as the alternative for platelet counts. Confirm by looking at the smear
Giant / large plateletsFalsely low platelet countToo large for the platelet size windowFluorescent (PLT-F) channel, which identifies by staining rather than size; smear review. Consider Bernard–Soulier syndrome
Schistocytes, microcytes, white cell fragmentsFalsely high platelet countSmall enough to fall into the platelet size windowFluorescent platelet count; smear review
Cold agglutinins (red cell agglutination)Falsely low RBC count, falsely high MCV, impossibly high MCHCClumped red cells are counted as one large cell. The Hct is calculated from RBC × MCV, so it falls; MCHC = Hgb/Hct rises absurdly. Flagged as "RBC agglutination"Warm the sample to 37 °C and re-run
Lipemia, marked leukocytosis, hyperbilirubinemiaFalsely high hemoglobin → falsely high MCH and MCHCTurbidity and pigment add absorbance at the reading wavelength. The 555 nm choice is specifically to minimise interference by turbidity and other compounds, but it cannot eliminate itPlasma replacement / blank correction; recognise that a very high MCHC is usually artefactual
Nucleated red blood cellsFalsely high white cell countThey have nuclei, so they land in the leukocyte gateModern analyzers count and subtract them automatically; otherwise correct the white count manually
Clotted specimenFalsely low platelet and cell countsCells are trapped in the clot and never reach the apertureReject and redraw — "no clots or clumps" is an explicit acceptance criterion
Delayed or refrigerated specimenUnreliable indices, especially MCVCells swell over time. Ideal ≤3 hours, acceptable ≤8 hours; refrigerated samples beyond that may degradeRedraw
🪝 The single best artefact detector: an MCHC above ~37 g/dL

MCHC is a concentration, and a red cell can only hold so much hemoglobin per unit volume — the normal range tops out around 37 g/dL. So a reported MCHC well above that is almost never a real biological finding. It means either the hemoglobin was read too high (lipemia, very high white count, hyperbilirubinemia) or the hematocrit was calculated too low (cold agglutinins clumping red cells). Both point straight at a specimen problem.

The one genuine exception worth knowing: hereditary spherocytosis, where cells really are hyperdense — a high MCHC there is a clue, not an error.

🩺 Lecture summary — the closing slide
  • CBCs are one of the most common tests performed.
  • Sophisticated automated hematology analyzers provide a great deal of information and can flag abnormal samples.
  • White cell, red cell and platelet counts and metrics are all used to diagnose blood disorders.
  • The pathologist can help interpret interferences and determine whether results are consistent with other findings from the patient.
  • In some cases, you may need to redraw the specimen.

Q: A CBC on an elderly patient reports RBC 1.9 ×106/µL, MCV 128 fL, Hgb 11.8 g/dL, Hct 24.3%, MCHC 48.6 g/dL. What is going on, and what should the laboratory do?

Answer

Cold agglutinins causing red cell agglutination. The giveaway is the MCHC of 48.6 g/dL — far above the normal ceiling of about 37 g/dL, and physically impossible.

The mechanism runs straight through the calculations: clumped red cells cross the aperture together and are counted as one very large cell, so the RBC count falls and the MCV rises. Because Hct = (RBC × MCV)/10 is calculated, and the count fell further than the volume rose, the hematocrit is falsely low — and since MCHC = (Hgb/Hct) × 100, the MCHC is driven absurdly high. The hemoglobin itself is measured on lysed cells and stays accurate.

The fix is to warm the sample to 37 °C and re-run it, which disperses the agglutinates. The analyzer should also have raised an "RBC agglutination" flag. Clinically, follow up with a cold agglutinin titre and a direct antiglobulin test.

Q: An asymptomatic outpatient has a platelet count of 22,000/µL on an EDTA sample. There is no bleeding. What is the most likely explanation and what is the next step?

Answer

EDTA-dependent platelet clumping — pseudothrombocytopenia. A count that low with no bleeding at all is the clue: genuine severe thrombocytopenia usually shows petechiae or mucosal bleeding.

The mechanism is the impedance size window again: platelet clumps are too large to be counted as platelets and are missed, or misread as white cells. The analyzer should have flagged "Platelet clumps?"

Next steps: look at the smear to confirm clumping directly, then redraw in a citrate (blue top) tube — named in the specimen criteria as the alternative for platelet counts, because the antibody responsible is EDTA-dependent. A fluorescent (PLT-F) platelet count is also useful, since it identifies platelets by staining rather than by size.

Reference

Glossary and Abbreviations

Every abbreviation and technical term used in this file, written out and defined.

The count and its indices
CBC — complete blood count
The panel reporting red cell, white cell, platelet and (optionally) reticulocyte parameters. One of the most commonly ordered tests in medicine.
RBC — red blood cell (erythrocyte)
The oxygen-carrying cell. Normal count 3.5–5.5 ×106/µL. Measured directly by impedance.
WBC — white blood cell (leukocyte)
The immune cells. Counted by impedance; the differential comes from flow cytometry.
Hgb — hemoglobin
The oxygen-carrying protein, and the value that defines anemia. Measured photometrically at 555 nm. Normal 14–18 g/dL (male), 12–16 g/dL (female).
Hct — hematocrit
Proportion of blood volume occupied by red cells. Traditionally measured by centrifugation; on an analyzer calculated as (RBC × MCV)/10. Normal 40–50% (male), 36–48% (female).
MCV — mean corpuscular volume
Average red cell size, in femtolitres. Measured from impedance pulse height. Normal 80–100 fL; lower in children. The first branch of the anemia algorithm.
MCH — mean corpuscular hemoglobin
The average amount of hemoglobin per cell. Calculated as (Hgb/RBC) × 10. Normal 26–34 pg/cell.
MCHC — mean corpuscular hemoglobin concentration
Hemoglobin density within the cell. Calculated as (Hgb/Hct) × 100. Normal 31–37 g/dL. A value well above 37 is usually an artefact.
RDW — red cell distribution width
Variation in red cell size. Calculated as SD of volume / MCV. Normal 11.4–14.5. A raised RDW with a normal MCV suggests two populations.
MPV — mean platelet volume
Average platelet size, from impedance.
Reticulocyte
An immature red cell that has lost its nucleus but still contains RNA. Counted with an RNA stain; normal 0.8–4%. Distinguishes decreased production from increased destruction.
Immature platelet fraction
The platelet equivalent of the reticulocyte count — newly released platelets, measured on the fluorescent channel.
fL — femtolitre
10−15 litres. The unit of MCV.
pg — picogram
10−12 grams. The unit of MCH.
Methods and instruments
Coulter principle (impedance)
A cell crossing an aperture changes electrical impedance; each pulse is one cell, and pulse height is proportional to size. Gives RBC count + MCV, platelet count + MPV, and the WBC count.
Flow cytometry
Separates cells by forward scatter (size) and side scatter (complexity/granularity). The basis of the automated white cell differential.
SLS — sodium lauryl sulfate
The cyanide-free hemoglobin reagent. Lyses cells, oxidises heme, and forms a stable coloured SLS-HGB complex read at 555 nm.
PLT-F — fluorescent platelet channel
Stains platelet rough endoplasmic reticulum and mitochondria with oxazine and counts by fluorescence rather than size. Correlates with CD41/CD61; especially useful below 50 ×103/µL.
Sysmex XN-2000 / XN-1000
The hematology analyzers described; they count about 36,000 cells per sample.
CellaVision
A microscope scanner that rapidly captures cell images and pre-classifies leukocytes for technologist confirmation. Requires a consistently made smear.
HemaPrep
An automated smear spreader producing the consistent smear CellaVision needs.
Accuracy
Closeness to the "true" result. Reduced by systematic bias, which may indicate an instrument problem.
Precision
Reproducibility over time. Reduced by random bias, which may be an intrinsic feature of the assay.
Autoverification
Automatic release of results when there are no flags and values are near normal, without human review.
EDTA — ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid
The lavender-top anticoagulant for the CBC; binds calcium irreversibly. Contrast with the reversible citrate used for coagulation testing. K2 and K3 refer to the potassium salt used.
Wright–Giemsa stain
The peripheral smear stain, combining eosin and methylene blue. Devised in 1902; named for James Homer Wright and Gustav Giemsa.
Hematoxylin
A basic dye that stains acidic material such as nuclear DNA — blue/purple.
Eosin
An acidic dye that stains basic material such as cytoplasmic protein — pink/orange.
Monolayer
The region of a smear where cells are evenly distributed without touching or overlapping — the only place morphology should be assessed.
Feather edge
The thin trailing end of a smear, where cells are distorted and large cells collect.
Morphology
Microcyte
A red cell smaller than normal (MCV <80 fL). Iron deficiency, thalassemia, lead poisoning, sideroblastic anemia.
Macrocyte
A red cell larger than normal (MCV >100 fL). B12 or folate deficiency, liver disease.
Anisocytosis
Variation in red cell size — microcytes and macrocytes together. Reflected in a raised RDW.
Hypochromia
Fainter staining showing reduced hemoglobin content; the central pallor occupies more than a third of the cell.
Poikilocytosis
Variation in red cell shape (as distinct from anisocytosis, which is size).
Polychromasia
Larger, blue-grey red cells on the smear — reticulocytes. Indicates the marrow is responding.
Spherocyte
Small, round, densely staining cell with no central pallor. Hereditary spherocytosis; autoimmune hemolytic anemia.
Ovalocyte / elliptocyte
Oval or cigar-shaped red cell. Hereditary elliptocytosis; also iron deficiency and myelodysplasia.
Stomatocyte
Red cell whose central pallor is a slit or "mouth". Hereditary stomatocytosis; alcohol and liver disease.
Dacryocyte (tear drop cell)
Red cell with one pointed end. Myelofibrosis, marrow infiltration, thalassemia.
Codocyte (target cell)
Red cell with a central dot of hemoglobin inside the pallor — a bullseye. Excess membrane relative to contents: thalassemia, hemoglobin C, liver disease, post-splenectomy.
Acanthocyte (spur cell)
Red cell with few, irregular, unevenly spaced blunt projections. Severe liver disease, abetalipoproteinemia.
Echinocyte (burr cell)
Red cell with many, regular, evenly spaced short spicules. Uremia — and a common preparation artefact.
Schistocyte
A red cell fragment without central pallor and with two pointed ends. Marks a microangiopathic hemolytic anemia.
Sickle cell
Rigid crescent-shaped red cell of sickle cell disease, from β6 Glu→Val polymerisation of deoxygenated hemoglobin S.
Nucleated red blood cell
An immature red cell retaining its nucleus. Falsely raises the automated white cell count unless corrected.
Left shift
Increased immature granulocytes (bands, metamyelocytes, myelocytes) in the blood — typically a marrow responding to infection or inflammation.
Clinical terms
TIBC — total iron binding capacity
A measure of available transferrin binding sites. Rises in iron deficiency. Normal 160–415 mcg/dL.
Ferritin
The iron storage protein; the best single marker of iron stores. Normal 10–500 ng/mL; very low in true iron deficiency. Note it is also an acute-phase reactant.
Hemoglobin electrophoresis
Separates hemoglobin variants by charge; used to diagnose sickle cell disease, thalassemia and hemoglobin variants such as hemoglobin E and hemoglobin C.
Sickle solubility test
A rapid screen in which deoxygenated hemoglobin S precipitates and makes the solution turbid. Screening only — it does not distinguish trait from disease.
Hydroxyurea
Maintenance therapy in sickle cell disease; raises fetal hemoglobin, which interferes with hemoglobin S polymerisation.
Acute chest syndrome
A pulmonary complication of sickle cell disease with a new infiltrate plus respiratory symptoms; a leading cause of death.
Splenic sequestration
Acute pooling of blood in the spleen in sickle cell disease, causing rapid anemia and hypovolaemia.
MAHA — microangiopathic hemolytic anemia
Red cell destruction by mechanical shearing in small vessels, producing schistocytes.
TTP — thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura
A microangiopathy from ADAMTS13 failure. Schistocytes and thrombocytopenia with normal PT and aPTT.
HUS — hemolytic uremic syndrome
A predominantly renal microangiopathy, classically from Shiga toxin–producing E. coli.
DIC — disseminated intravascular coagulation
Systemic coagulation activation. Schistocytes plus prolonged PT and aPTT and falling fibrinogen — the distinction from a microangiopathy.
March hemoglobinuria
Mechanical red cell destruction from repetitive impact, such as prolonged marching or running.
Plasmodium
The malaria parasite. P. falciparum is the most virulent and can exceed 10% parasitaemia; P. vivax, P. malariae and P. ovale share a common antigen on the BinaxNOW rapid test.
Parasitaemia
The percentage of red cells infected. Reported with every malaria smear; drives treatment intensity and monitors response.
Cold agglutinin
An antibody that clumps red cells at low temperature, causing a falsely low RBC count, falsely high MCV and an impossibly high MCHC. Resolved by warming the sample to 37 °C.
Pseudothrombocytopenia
A falsely low platelet count from EDTA-dependent platelet clumping. Confirmed on the smear; resolved by redrawing into citrate.
Lipemia
Turbid, fat-laden plasma. Raises absorbance and therefore falsely raises the measured hemoglobin.

🎯 CBC & Blood Smears — High-Yield One-Pager

Cyril Jacquot, MD · condensed by learning objective — components & workflow · methodology · diagnostic information · interferences

LO 1–2 · METHOD

Specimen rules

  • EDTA (lavender); ideal ≤3 h, acceptable ≤8 h
  • No clots or clumps
  • Citrate (blue) is the alternative for platelet counts
  • BD vs Greiner tube: MCV/RDW/Hct 1–2% higher, not clinically significant

Four measurement principles

  • Impedance (Coulter) → RBC + MCV, PLT + MPV, WBC count. Pulse = one cell; height = size
  • Flow cytometry → differential. Forward = size, side = complexity
  • SLS photometry at 555 nm → hemoglobin (cyanide-free)
  • Fluorescence (oxazine, PLT-F) → platelets by content, not size; matches CD41/CD61

Measured vs calculated

  • Measured: RBC, MCV, Hgb
  • Calculated: Hct = RBC×MCV/10; MCH = Hgb/RBC×10; MCHC = Hgb/Hct×100; RDW = SD/MCV
  • ★ Rule of three: Hct ≈ 3 × Hgb (if MCV normal)
  • Errors in measured values propagate

Accuracy vs precision

  • Systematic bias → ↓accuracy → suspect the instrument
  • Random bias → ↓precision → may be intrinsic to the assay
  • Platelets vary 15–20% intrinsically; MCV very tight
  • Analyzer counts ~36,000 cells/sample
LO 3 · DIAGNOSIS

Normal ranges

  • RBC 3.5–5.5 ×106/µL
  • Hgb 14–18 (M) / 12–16 (F) g/dL
  • MCV 80–100 fL (lower in children)
  • Hct 40–50 (M) / 36–48 (F) %
  • MCH 26–34 pg · MCHC 31–37 g/dL · RDW 11.4–14.5
  • Reticulocytes 0.8–4%

Anemia algorithm

  • MCV <80: iron, thalassemia (↑RBC count!), Hgb E, metal toxicity, (chronic disease, sideroblastic)
  • MCV 80–100, ↓retics: renal failure, chronic disease, sideroblastic, hypoendocrine, aplastic, mixed
  • MCV 80–100, ↑retics: hemolysis, recovery, hemoglobinopathy, enzymopathy, membranopathy
  • MCV >100: megaloblastic, alcohol, drugs, liver, hypothyroid, myelodysplasia

⚠ MCV is an average

  • Normal MCV + ↑RDW → dual population
  • Seen with brisk reticulocytosis or after transfusion
  • Confirm on the smear

Stains

  • Cells are translucent without stain
  • Hematoxylin = basic dye → acidic DNA (blue)
  • Eosin = acidic dye → basic protein (pink)
  • Wright–Giemsa = eosin + methylene blue, 1902
  • Read the monolayer, not the feather edge
  • Normal central pallor ≈ 1/3 of the cell
LO 3–4 · CASES & ARTEFACT

The four cases

  • Microcytic/hypochromic, Hgb 3.6, ferritin 1, ↑TIBC → iron deficiency; ferrous sulfate + restrict milk
  • Sickle + target cells, polychromasia → HbSS; β6 Glu→Val; fever = ceftriaxone
  • Schistocytes + ↓platelets + confusion → TTP
  • Fever + travel + ↓platelets → malaria; report parasitaemia %
  • Target cells → send hemoglobin electrophoresis
  • TTP pentad: fever, ↓plt, MAHA, neuro, renal — treat before all five

Morphology → disease

  • Spherocytes → HS, autoimmune hemolysis
  • Target cells → thalassemia, HbC, liver, splenectomy
  • Tear drops → myelofibrosis
  • Acanthocyte (few, irregular) → liver
  • Echinocyte (many, even) → uremia / artefact
  • Schistocyte → TTP, HUS, DIC, valves, malignant HTN
  • Stomatocyte → alcohol, liver

★ Interferences

  • Platelet clumps / giant platelets → falsely LOW platelets → citrate tube, PLT-F
  • Schistocytes, microcytes, WBC fragments → falsely HIGH platelets
  • Cold agglutinins → ↓RBC, ↑MCV, ↑↑MCHC → warm to 37 °C
  • Lipemia / high WBC / bilirubin → falsely high Hgb
  • Nucleated RBCs → falsely high WBC
  • MCHC >37 g/dL is almost always artefact (exception: hereditary spherocytosis)

Master reference — every index, how it is obtained, and what makes it lie
